newsitem.title: USA: Alternatives to official U.S. presidential debates.
newsitem.headline: Alternatives to official U.S. presidential debates.

text.p: It's official: only Bob Dole and Bill Clinton will take part in the regular presidential debates. But there are plenty of alternative forums, in print, possibly on radio and certainly on the World Wide Web.

While Democratic President Clinton and former Senate Republican leader Dole slug it out on live television starting at 9 p.m. EDT Sunday, (0100 GMT Monday) Reform Party candidate Ross Perot will start two hours earlier with a paid informercial on the ABC network.

Perot's paid half-hour program will be followed at 10:30 p.m. EDT (0230 GMT) by a 45-minute appearance on CNN's "Larry King Live", in which the Texas billionaire will answer the same questions posed to the major party candidates during their debate and be bound by the same strict time limitations.
This plan was adopted when the courts upheld a decision by the Commission on Presidential Debates to bar Perot from the official match-up, said Perot spokeswoman Micheau Jaderlund.
"That was the only offer he had," Jaderlund said by telephone. "This was the only invitation we had to get our message out to the voters."

Perot's running mate, economist Pat Choate, will appear on the CNN program on Wednesday, following the regular vice presidential debate between Republican Jack Kemp and Democratic Vice President Al Gore, the spokeswoman said.

The nation's radio talk show hosts, spearheaded by conservative host Michael Reagan, have invited Clinton and Dole to participate in a debate on their airwaves, promising to reach 100 percent of the U.S. radio market.

"We believe talk radio hosts, who listen to the views of the American people on a daily basis, are also well-qualified to ask questions to help Americans make their important decision on Election Day," Reagan, son of former President Ronald Reagan, wrote to Dole and Clinton.

Both Dole and Kemp have appeared on Reagan's four-hour show, which is distributed to 125 radio stations, and have made positive comments about the radio debate, but producer Paul Wilkinson said it was unlikely to happen this year.

"Probably the most constructive thing is that it's on the table this time and four years from now we can get a little more consideration ... either as a separate debate or as part of the current format," Reagan's producer Wilkinson said by telephone.

Even the regular debate need not be viewed on television. An audio feed of the 90-minute contest will be heard in real-time along with text transcripts of the debate on the World Wide Web at http://www.debate96.net.

There will also be commentary by Larry Williams, editor at the Hartford Courant newspaper, which is sponsoring the website along with ZipLink, which designed the site. Two Connecticut state legislators will also be available to comment.
Those who visit the site will be able to vote on candidate performance as it occurs, with results available soon after the debate concludes, ZipLink said in a statement.

But not all attempts at an alternative exchange of views work well. In Chicago, the Sun-Times newspaper complained in a front-page story on Friday that its attempt to let Clinton and Dole speak their minds in back-to-back 2,000 word essays was a failure. The Sun-Times printed the responses last week.

"What the candidates gave us was old material recycled word for word," said Editor-in-Chief Nigel Wade. "Clinton and Dole had several months in which to take Illinois voters more seriously than they did ... Voters are electing a president, not a word-processor. They want dialogue -- what they got was voice mail."

If the live debate on Sunday leaves viewers and listeners cold, they can go for relief to http://www.debate96.org, a website that features transcripts of presidential debates of yesteryear, starting with the 1960 debate between Republican Richard Nixon and Democrat John F. Kennedy.
